stories.topic: Larry Summers: from a car phone to a river in Africa
stories.summary: Ajay retells what Larry Summers calls the most dramatic technical change of his life. Ajay places it around the 1992 US elections, when Summers was advising Michael Dukakis at a Democratic convention that Ajay thinks was in Chicago. A car sent to pick Summers up had a phone in it. He had never seen one before, so he picked it up and called his wife to tell her he was calling from a car. A scant year and a half later he was crossing a river in Africa when someone handed him a GSM phone and said, 'This call is for you.'
stories.insight: When a technology rides a falling price curve, democratisation is measured in months, not generations. The exotic toy of the rich becomes ordinary kit in the remotest places almost immediately.
stories.quote: He says it took one and a half years to reach from some exotic technology in America to a river crossing in Africa.

stories.topic: A whole university on one T1 line
stories.summary: When Ajay was a PhD student in America, the entire University of Southern California ran on a single T1 line of about 1.5 megabits a second, and that was considered the height of cool. Today an ordinary home connection gives something like 300 megabits a second, at a price lower than what was paid for that T1 line.
stories.insight: Bandwidth is one of the 'Moore's Laws' of price. What was once a whole institution's prized resource is now an unnoticed household utility, and that is the kind of change we tend to normalise and forget.
stories.quote: An entire university ran on 1.5 megabits a second.

stories.topic: The startup killed by its own success
stories.summary: In 2000, after the Nasdaq crash scared off the investors in his first startup, and while Kaun Banega Crorepati was becoming a hit, Amit built Crow Master. It was a gamified online quiz with a quizmaster called Babu Moshai, running on thousands of questions written by paid quizzer friends, and it was part of a site called Mindfever.com. Because the game was interactive, he hosted it on VSNL to keep the server close to users, and VSNL charged by traffic. The game went viral, and for one month it was the number two site in India, between Rediff and Cricinfo. A buyout interest from Star's Bangalore digital arm fell through when that arm shut down. The traffic bill put him heavily into debt, and the site closed after about three months.
stories.insight: The same metric can bankrupt you or make you, depending on where you sit on the cost curve. In 2000, success in user acquisition was ruinous. Today no startup fears traffic, because nobody pays for it that way anymore.
stories.quote: But that one month bankrupted us and took us hugely into debt because we were paying according to the traffic.

stories.topic: One perfect pot vs ten pots a day
stories.summary: Amit cites an experiment whose details he admits he has forgotten. One group was told to spend a month crafting a single perfect pot. The other was told to make ten pots a day, and their best would be judged. The perfectionists' pot came out mediocre, while the volume group quickly passed that standard and went on to make really good pots.
stories.insight: This is Wright's Law for creators: excellence comes from cumulative doing, not from agonising over one artefact. It is why Amit keeps urging creators to have a bias for action.
stories.quote: And then your baseline level gets so high that excellence automatically emerges.

stories.summary: Drawing on a Twitter thread by Ben Wolff, Amit describes how Horst Schulze, leading the Ritz-Carlton in 1983, let every employee from top to bottom spend up to $2,000 of the hotel's money on a guest without asking anyone. His reasoning was that a regular guest was worth $200,000 over a lifetime. Amit gives four examples. An employee flew from Atlanta to Hawaii himself to deliver a laptop a guest had left behind. Staff returned a child's forgotten Thomas the Tank Engine along with photos of Thomas enjoying spa treatment. When a couple lost their wedding ring on a Cancun beach the day before the wedding, an employee bought four metal detectors and had staff search all night until it was found. A server who overheard diners planning a conference at another hotel comped their $600 dinner, and they moved the conference to the Ritz, where it was held every year after that.
stories.insight: Incentives and trust turn employees who would otherwise go through the motions into owners who show initiative. The payoff is hard to measure but very real.
stories.quote: $2,000 was a very small amount of money to make people feel that this was their place.

stories.topic: An upgrade on the day his mother died
stories.summary: In 2008, when Amit's mother died, the family was flying back. At the airport counter one of them happened to mention it, and the woman at the counter, who had no need to do anything, gave them a free upgrade to business class. Amit thinks the airline was Jet, which no longer exists.
stories.insight: One small act of discretion by a frontline employee can create lifelong loyalty, which is the human side of the argument for empowering staff.
stories.quote: I thought it's beautiful. I thought I'm going to fly this airline forever.

stories.topic: ASML's decade-early bet on extreme ultraviolet
stories.summary: ASML in Holland makes what Ajay calls arguably the most complex machines on earth. Projecting along Moore's Law ten years ahead, it saw that conventional lithography would max out and that chipmaking would need extreme ultraviolet light, at around 13.5 nanometres. Nobody knew how to do it, and there were severe physics problems. Other firms that tried failed. ASML kept investing for years ahead of demand and got through.
stories.insight: A shared belief in the curve gives firms the closest thing to an assurance that a huge, risky, long-horizon investment will find a market. That is how Moore's Law keeps fulfilling itself.
stories.quote: Ten years ahead of time, projecting through Moore's Law, they saw the problem that conventional lithography was not going to work.

stories.summary: Paul Ehrlich made Malthusian predictions: Britain would be extinct by 2000, and half of India would starve by the end of the decade. Economist Julian Simon thought these claims were ridiculous. In 1980 they bet on the prices of five materials chosen by Ehrlich over ten years. Malthusian logic said a rising population would push prices up. Instead all five fell, and Simon won.
stories.insight: Population growth adds innovators, not just consumers. Prices fell because people kept innovating, which is the core of the 'people are brains, not stomachs' view.
stories.quote: Julian Simon was like, No, hold on, man. We are innovative, we are creative, that is a core of progress.

stories.topic: The fiber-optic glut that wasn't a waste
stories.summary: Around 2000, big companies sank more than $100 billion into laying fiber-optic cable across America, expecting the boom to continue. The dot-com bust left about 90% of that capacity unused. Companies went under and people called it a waste. But because the capacity physically existed, innovators built on it: broadband, mobile telephony and cloud computing. Today 80 to 90% of it is in use.
stories.insight: Overbuilt capacity is not necessarily waste. Once a constraint is lifted, human ingenuity fills the space, and the losses are part of healthy creative destruction.
stories.quote: Less than 10% of it is being used. But was it a waste?

stories.topic: Missing the curve on digital cameras and batteries
stories.summary: At the dawn of digital photography Ajay was a hardcore analog photographer, shooting Kodachrome and Ektachrome on Nikons and loving his slides. The engineer in him loved the idea of files, but early digital gear looked hopelessly shabby. Good images seemed to need about 12 megapixels, and the human fovea resolves something like 10,000 dots per inch. The gap seemed insuperable. He made the same mistake with lithium-ion batteries: although he and Ayush Patnaik spent many evenings dreaming about batteries, he didn't see the straight line in the semi-log graph, and today's battery miracles surprised him.
stories.insight: Even enthusiasts underestimate exponential improvement. Today's gap is the wrong thing to stare at; the slope is what matters.
stories.quote: And I failed to see that look, you just have to give it ten, twenty years, and these gaps will be overcome.

stories.summary: Van Morrison went to record Astral Weeks with a couple of musicians of his own, but the producer quickly sacked them and brought in his own crew, including the bassist Richard Davis. Morrison sang and played guitar while jazz musicians he didn't know improvised around him. He wasn't happy at first because it didn't match the picture in his head, but over time he came to see it as a masterpiece. Amit recalls that about thirty years later Morrison toured with Davis and wanted him to play the parts exactly as on the album. Davis refused, saying he was a jazz player and would do something different each time.
stories.insight: Sometimes the best work comes from losing control and letting other people's improvisation in. The creator is not always the best judge of his own work in the moment.
stories.quote: it was a bunch of jazz guys improvising. And the result is an absolute masterpiece.

core_ideas.concept: A CPU at heart: fetch, add, branch
core_ideas.explanation: The Intel 4004 was the world's first CPU on a single chip, and it did the whole job with about 2,300 transistors, where earlier CPUs were room-sized. At heart a CPU is a Turing machine that needs only three things: fetch a memory cell into a register, add, and branch on an 'if'. Today we casually spend billions of transistors.
core_ideas.quote: it needs to have an if to be able to branch. Everything else is toppings.

core_ideas.concept: Moore's Law is an economic law, not a law of physics
core_ideas.explanation: Gordon Moore's 1965 paper used just seven data points to observe that the number of transistors on a chip doubles roughly every 18 months. The industry itself was pushed into being by NASA's hunger for compact equipment on satellites. Nothing in nature guarantees the doubling. It holds because people keep piling on innovation and capital. Plotted on a semi-log graph (linear time, log y-axis), it is a straight line, which means a tenfold rise every few years.
core_ideas.quote: This is not a physics law. Right? There's no deeper reason why this ought to happen. It's not a physical fact about the universe. It's a social fact. It's an economic fact.

core_ideas.concept: Moore's Laws (plural): put price on the y-axis
core_ideas.explanation: Billions of transistors would be an exotic curiosity if each chip cost a million dollars. Ajay argues the more important version, perhaps five times more important, puts price or performance-per-price on the y-axis. That also gives straight semi-log lines, in solar panels, bandwidth, lithium-ion batteries, DNA sequencing and launch costs, where people now predict about $10 per kg to near-earth orbit. Our eyes should learn to spot these lines.
core_ideas.quote: As an economist, I just want to say that's the whole enchilada. You've got to get the prices down.

core_ideas.concept: From mechanical cleverness to trivial software
core_ideas.explanation: Cruise control and automatic transmission were once peaks of mechanical engineering that needed very clever people. With cheap CPUs they become a few lines of code: nudge the speed up or down around a target, or pick a gear from elevation and velocity. Ubiquitous cheap computation turns hard engineering problems into easy ones.
core_ideas.quote: Once you shift from a mechanical engineering worldview to a computational worldview, these things become easy.

core_ideas.explanation: Lighting went from candles to gas lamps, tungsten, fluorescent and LEDs, rising from roughly 9% to 90% efficiency. That happened through discontinuous jumps separated by stagnation, and now the journey is essentially over. Moore's Law is different: relentless improvement every year. Amit maps this onto learning, which can be continuous accumulation or a quantum leap followed by refinement and then another leap.
core_ideas.quote: What we are describing as Moore's Law is just this madness of grinding away year after year, the damn thing gets better, and you get straight lines in semi-log graphs.

core_ideas.concept: More transistors doesn't mean faster CPUs
core_ideas.explanation: CPUs were built around the single-threaded PDP-11 model, which chokes because the chip mostly waits on memory fetches. Tricks like speculative branch prediction, which computes both sides of an 'if', squeezed out about 10x and then maxed out. The resolution was the GPU: a thousand small parallel processors on one chip, with humans left to learn how to use them.
core_ideas.quote: Just adding transistors doesn't make your CPUs faster.

core_ideas.concept: Three rival laws of progress: time, lifetime volume, annual scale
core_ideas.explanation: Moore's Law puts time on the x-axis. Wright's Law (1936, from a man who was not one of the Wright brothers) puts cumulative lifetime output there, with roughly a 20% productivity gain for every doubling, also called the learning or experience curve. Goddard's Law puts annual production there, which is plain economies of scale. Across 62 industries, Nagy et al. found Wright's Law the best predictor. So think of a person or firm by lifetime output: the cobbler who has repaired 53,000 shoes, or the Indian doctor who has seen huge numbers of patients.
core_ideas.quote: Not time. Volume. You put in volume and you will get improvements.

core_ideas.concept: Bias for action: perfection is the enemy of production
core_ideas.explanation: For creators, Wright's Law means volume beats polishing. Many get stuck trying to make the perfect blog or episode. Amit's case is that doing over and over raises your baseline until excellence emerges.
core_ideas.quote: But the key to excellence is not to spend forever over trying to make something perfect, but doing, doing, doing, doing, doing.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit adds the qualifier from Anders Ericsson, popularised by Malcolm Gladwell: volume alone is not enough. A boy at the cricket nets can mindlessly hit balls for half an hour, or he can work on footwork, elbow position, balance and a still head, internalising one quality at a time.
core_ideas.quote: It is not just enough to do do do blindly, like an automaton like what you've described, but deliberate practice.

core_ideas.concept: Wright's Law is earned, not given
core_ideas.explanation: The learning curve is a frontier, not a guarantee. Gains come from purposive 'manufacturing excellence'. Ajay sees this on the Britannia board, where the company squeezes out energy savings and lower wastage every year. His test for any firm is to plot productivity against cumulative volume on a log scale. If there is no straight line, something is wrong with the organisation.
core_ideas.quote: If not, something is wrong with your organization, something is wrong with your culture.

core_ideas.concept: Why bad firms add volume but don't learn
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay names three failure modes. Workers operate consultant-chosen machines like helpless peasants and wait for the next upgrade instead of improving the process. Teams churn, so tacit knowledge walks out the door. And firms are cut to the bone, with a pure 'shut up and execute' culture that leaves no slack for thinking, debate, experiments or mistakes. Lean looks efficient in the short run but kills the journey to quality.
core_ideas.quote: But when you lack the fat, thinking, for strategy, for innovation, for making mistakes. Then actually you don't get on these journeys to quality.

core_ideas.concept: I, CPU: Moore's Law as a coordination mechanism
core_ideas.explanation: Making a chip involves ASML's machines in Holland, three American firms' chip-design software, tens of thousands of engineers in Bangalore, and ARM, Apple, Intel and hundreds of others. That is a huge coordination problem, and Mahalanobis-style thinking says only a coercive government could solve it. Yet no government does. The shared, near-religious belief in the 18-month doubling lets firms invest ahead of each other in sync, making the law self-fulfilling. Amit's addition: articulating the law matters as much as the law itself, because the shared dream is what makes action look coordinated.
core_ideas.quote: So Moore's Law has this very interesting idea that it's a bit of a self-fulfilling prophecy. It became a coordination mechanism by hundreds of firms.

core_ideas.concept: Build for tomorrow's cost curve, not today's
core_ideas.explanation: Today's AI spending is outrageous and unprofitable. At about fifty paise per Gemini API call, most Indian app ideas don't pay. Ajay says innovators must imagine the world when that falls to 0.05 paise and build for it, like a science-fiction writer. Amit says the same to entrepreneurs, citing Netflix betting on streaming in 2007 before bandwidth and displays were ready.
core_ideas.quote: Make for the future. Don't make for today. Today will be an artifact by the time twenty-four hours are over

core_ideas.concept: Humans are bad at exponential thinking
core_ideas.explanation: Having misjudged digital cameras and batteries himself, Ajay warns that we all underrate straight lines on semi-log graphs. The habit to build is to keep scanning industries for Wright's-law curves and ask what you would do with them, since they are happening all around us and ignoring them is dangerous.
core_ideas.quote: So I would like to say to everybody that humans are not good at exponential thinking.

core_ideas.explanation: Against the claim that new technology widens inequality, Amit asks for evidence. Technology starts with governments or the rich, as GPS went from military and space use to luxury cars, and then reaches everyone. AI is usable by anyone today, and falling prices are what make this democratisation happen.
core_ideas.quote: The cell phone that I use is not very different from the cell phone Elon Musk uses.

core_ideas.explanation: Each time an energy source looked exhausted, scarcity raised prices and triggered innovation. As forests thinned, wood gave way to coal. Whale oil, with its race for better ships, extraction and storage, gave way to fossil fuels. Nuclear and renewables now promise a way beyond those. Amit argues the deepest fact about humans is endless innovation, and the Ehrlich–Simon bet is evidence for it.
core_ideas.quote: Like the core truth about human beings is that we are innovative, that we can innovate endlessly.

core_ideas.concept: Lift the constraints and humans fill the space
core_ideas.explanation: Capacity built for one purpose gets repurposed by human imagination. Overbuilt fiber became the backbone of broadband and the cloud. GPS, made for the military, now gets your food delivered. Memory-foam pillows made for spacecraft are now in homes. Technology is downstream of human creativity.
core_ideas.quote: humans are incredible at maximizing within their constraints. As you lift those constraints, as those boundaries expand, as capacity expands, humans will innovate and fill that space.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: The cold open is a 'test of Ajay's math skills': the sum of the squares of the first four primes. Ajay adds 4, 9, 25 and 49 aloud and lands on 87, so Amit says 'Welcome to episode eighty seven.'

Amit refuses to let Ajay simply announce another topic: 'God knows how many episodes on firms you've gotten away with and other interesting subjects like bankruptcy regulation.' Ajay is interviewed like a job applicant. 'Applicant's name.' 'Moore's Laws.' 'Is your name Moore's Laws?' 'My father was Mr. Laws.' Age fifty-nine, occupation YouTuber. His pitch begins: 'There's a great wild west wind tearing through this modern world and it is called CPUs.' It ends with the question of whether the form must be submitted in triplicate: 'Yes, why not... in physical copies.'
Amit: 'Bollywood has always been fascinated by log graphs... there are songs about it.' It is a pun on 'log', the Hindi word for 'people'.

After the chessboard parable, Ajay works out the rice in kilograms against the mass of the earth and concludes it is 'well beyond the resources of any king.' Amit shrugs: 'Doesn't matter. It's a lot of grain.'

Ajay: 'for all ye callow gentle readers that are used to squandering like billions of transistors in the CPUs on your phones, I will have you know... the Intel 4004 had something like 2300 transistors.'

Amit: 'I am the best driver in Bombay partly because automatic transmission allows me to take my mind off' gear-shifting and onto 'optimal lane shifting'. He calls manual vs automatic 'a deeply ideological question, akin to the Oxford comma and the semicolon.'

On dial-up days, Amit recalls having 'half a picture of Samantha Fox' when the connection drops and the screen says buffering, while the edit plays the modem sound: 'Just as you are seeing now, gentle reader, we are so smart.' Ajay tops it: 'I could listen to the negotiation of the modem and I would know which protocol it got through.'

Amit applies Wright's Law to the show: 'when we make episode one seventy four will be twenty percent better than we are now.' Ajay agrees, and notes the bulk of the gains came early and 'now the learning rate has gone down.'
In the Ritz-Carlton story, Amit refuses to call Thomas the Tank Engine a toy because that would insult Thomas, and adds that the hotel sent photos of Thomas enjoying spa treatment.
Asked by Van Morrison decades later to replay his Astral Weeks bass lines exactly, Richard Davis replies, as Amit tells it: 'No, you fucker, I'm a jazz player, I'll do something different each time.'

The parable of the king and the chessboard: one grain of rice on the first square, doubled on each square after, which becomes an impossible amount by the 64th. It is used to show the power of doubling.
Kaun Banega Crorepati: the quiz show was becoming a hit in 2000, which is the context for Amit building his online quiz game.
'Classic Mahalanobis-based kind of thinking': Ajay's shorthand for the planner's belief that only a coercive government can coordinate a complex industry, which the semiconductor world disproves.
Ajay's riff on Leonard Read's essay: 'I, Pencil does not hold a candle to I, CPU.'

Brown Eyed Girl's line about going down to the old mine with a transistor radio. Amit first asks whether Ajay's wife Susan has brown eyes ('Little bit'), then recalls not realising as a kid that 'transistor' was short for transistor radio.

Transistor radios as the 'killer app' of the old days, glued to people's ears for cricket commentary. Amit notes that a generation's memories of Sunil Gavaskar's straight drive, or of Marshall being hit, were imagined from commentary and later retrofitted onto footage.
Netflix's 2007 bet on streaming, before the bandwidth and displays were good enough, is cited as the opposite of Ajay's digital-camera mistake.
